questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the sequence in which electrical impulses travel through the normal cardiac conduction system?
options: SA node → internodal tracts → AV node → Bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
AV node → SA node → internodal tracts → Bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
SA node → AV node → internodal tracts → Purkinje fibers → bundle branches → Bundle of His
SA node → internodal tracts → Bundle of His → AV node → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
questions.explanation:
The correct sequence is SA node → internodal tracts → AV node → Bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers, which represents the complete cardiac conduction pathway.
The SA node generates the initial impulse, which travels through the internodal tracts to reach the AV node. After a physiologic delay at the AV node, the impulse enters the Bundle of His, splits into the right and left bundle branches, and finally activates the Purkinje fiber network to depolarize the ventricles.
Option B begins at the AV node, making it the pacemaker rather than the SA node — incorrect.
Option C places the internodal tracts after the AV node; those tracts connect the SA node to the AV node, not the reverse.
Option D inserts the Bundle of His before the AV node, bypassing the essential AV nodal delay.
Slide 3 · Transcript 0:46

questions.text: Which of the following ECG findings is the defining characteristic that identifies a cardiac rhythm as a sinus rhythm?
options: A QRS complex preceding every P wave
A P wave preceding every QRS complex
A QRS rate between 60 and 100 beats per minute
Absence of ST segment changes in all leads
questions.explanation:
Sinus rhythm is defined by a P wave preceding every QRS complex, indicating that every heartbeat originates from the SA node.
When the SA node fires, atrial depolarization produces the P wave. The impulse then travels through the AV node and His-Purkinje system to activate the ventricles, producing the QRS. As long as the SA node controls the rhythm, a P wave precedes every QRS complex.
Option A reverses the sequence — a QRS before a P wave would indicate a junctional or ventricular origin, not sinus.
Option C describes a rate criterion that is unrelated to the definition of sinus rhythm; an escape rhythm at 45 bpm can still satisfy the sinus-rhythm definition if P waves precede each QRS.
Option D describes ST morphology, which is unrelated to whether the rhythm originates from the SA node.
Slide 4 · Transcript 1:46

questions.text: A 58-year-old man is evaluated for new-onset symptomatic bradycardia. Coronary angiography reveals significant stenosis in one vessel. In approximately 70% of individuals, which coronary vessel gives rise to the SA nodal artery?
options: Left anterior descending artery
Left circumflex artery
Right coronary artery
Posterior descending artery
questions.explanation:
The SA nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery (RCA) in approximately 70% of individuals, making RCA disease the most common culprit when SA node ischemia produces bradycardia or arrhythmia.
RCA ischemia can damage the SA node, producing tachyarrhythmias, bradyarrhythmias, or outright SA node failure. In the remaining ~30% of individuals the SA nodal artery arises from the left circumflex artery instead.
Option A, the left anterior descending artery, supplies the anterior wall and septum but does not typically give rise to the SA nodal artery.
Option B, the left circumflex, supplies the SA nodal artery only in the minority (~30%) of individuals.
Option D, the posterior descending artery, is a branch of the RCA that supplies the AV node — a different structure.
Slide 4 · Transcript 2:12

questions.text: A 62-year-old woman develops ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF during an acute coronary event. After reperfusion, her monitor shows P waves that are occasionally not followed by QRS complexes. Which vessel most directly supplies the cardiac node responsible for this new conduction disturbance?
options: Left anterior descending artery
SA nodal artery
Left circumflex artery
Posterior descending artery
questions.explanation:
The AV node is supplied by the posterior descending artery (PDA), a branch of the right coronary artery; PDA ischemia from an inferior MI can damage the AV node and cause atrioventricular conduction block.
The inferior MI pattern (ST elevation in II, III, aVF) signals RCA territory ischemia. When the PDA is compromised, the AV node loses its blood supply. AV nodal damage disrupts conduction between atria and ventricles, producing P waves that are not always followed by QRS complexes. PDA ischemia can also cause supraventricular arrhythmias.
Option A, the LAD, supplies the anterior wall and septum — not the AV node.
Option B, the SA nodal artery, supplies the SA node, not the AV node; SA node damage would typically affect rate, not produce dropped QRS complexes.
Option C, the left circumflex, supplies the SA nodal artery in ~30% of individuals but does not typically supply the AV node.
Slide 4 · Transcript 2:56

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the voltage-gating behavior of the funny current (If) channel that accounts for its role in SA nodal pacemaker activity?
options: Opens at hyperpolarized voltages (below approximately −60 mV) and closes as the membrane depolarizes
Opens at depolarized voltages (approximately −30 mV) and inactivates slowly over hundreds of milliseconds
Opens at approximately −50 mV and inactivates rapidly, contributing only briefly to depolarization
Remains continuously open and is regulated solely by intracellular calcium concentration
questions.explanation:
The funny (If) channel opens at hyperpolarized voltages below approximately −60 mV and closes as the SA node depolarizes — the reverse of most voltage-gated channels, which is why it is called "funny."
After each action potential, as the SA node repolarizes below −60 mV, If channels open and allow a mixed Na+/K+ current (with net inward Na+ flow) to enter the cell. This inward current slowly depolarizes the membrane toward threshold, driving the early component of Phase 4 depolarization. As voltage rises during Phase 4, the If channels close.
Option B describes L-type Ca2+ channel behavior — activating at more depolarized voltages (~−30 mV) with slow inactivation.
Option C describes T-type Ca2+ channel behavior — a threshold near −50 mV with rapid inactivation, distinct from the funny channel.
Option D is incorrect; the funny channel is voltage-gated and does not remain open at all voltages.
Slide 8 · Transcript 6:26

questions.text: In an SA nodal cell undergoing a spontaneous action potential, which of the following correctly orders the sequence of channel activations from initiation of Phase 4 through the upstroke?
options: T-type Ca2+ channels → funny current (If) channels → L-type Ca2+ channels
Funny current (If) channels → T-type Ca2+ channels → L-type Ca2+ channels
L-type Ca2+ channels → funny current (If) channels → T-type Ca2+ channels
Funny current (If) channels → L-type Ca2+ channels → T-type Ca2+ channels
questions.explanation:
The correct sequence is If → T-type Ca2+ → L-type Ca2+ channels, with each activation step driving the membrane toward the next channel's threshold.
At hyperpolarized voltages following repolarization, If channels open first and Na+ influx initiates early Phase 4 depolarization. As the membrane approaches approximately −50 mV, T-type Ca2+ channels activate and act as an electrical bridge between If and L-type Ca2+. Once voltage reaches approximately −30 mV, L-type Ca2+ channels open and drive the rapid Phase 0 upstroke.
Option A reverses the order of T-type and If; If opens first at hyperpolarized voltage, not T-type.
Option C begins with L-type channels, which activate last at the most depolarized voltage — they cannot initiate Phase 4.
Option D skips T-type channels and places L-type immediately after If, omitting the bridging role of T-type Ca2+ current in late Phase 4.
Slide 9 · Transcript 8:52

questions.text: A pharmacologist selectively blocks L-type Ca2+ channels in isolated SA nodal cells. Which of the following best describes the primary direct effect on SA nodal electrical activity?
options: Phase 4 depolarization slows markedly because L-type Ca2+ channels drive the early pacemaker current
Both Phase 4 depolarization and the action potential upstroke are abolished
The action potential upstroke is abolished while Phase 4 depolarization continues
No effect occurs because SA nodal cells do not rely on Ca2+ channels for any phase of the action potential
questions.explanation:
L-type Ca2+ current generates the rapid upstroke (Phase 0) of the SA node action potential but does not contribute to the pacemaker current (Phase 4 depolarization), so blocking L-type channels eliminates the upstroke while Phase 4 continues.
Phase 4 depolarization in SA nodal cells is driven by the funny current (If, via Na+ influx) and T-type Ca2+ current — not L-type Ca2+ channels. L-type channels activate only at approximately −30 mV, which corresponds to the action potential threshold reached at the end of Phase 4. Their activation drives the upstroke, not the slow buildup of Phase 4.
Option A incorrectly attributes Phase 4 to L-type channels; If carries the early pacemaker current and continues unaffected.
Option B is incorrect for the same reason — L-type channel blockade cannot abolish Phase 4 because L-type channels do not contribute to it.
Option D is incorrect; SA nodal cells depend entirely on Ca2+ channels (both T-type and L-type) for Phase 0 and for the late portion of Phase 4.
Slide 8 · Transcript 7:48

questions.text: Which of the following lists correctly identifies all cardiac structures that possess intrinsic pacemaker (automaticity) activity?
options: SA node and AV node only
SA node, AV node, and ventricular myocardium
SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, and atrial myocardium
SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers
questions.explanation:
Intrinsic pacemaker activity exists in the SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers — not in the atrial or ventricular myocardium.
These five structures all have the capacity for spontaneous Phase 4 depolarization and can generate action potentials independently. Under normal conditions the SA node dominates because it has the fastest intrinsic rate and suppresses the others. The atrial and ventricular working myocardium have no intrinsic automaticity — they respond only to impulses delivered from the conduction system.
Option A omits the Bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers, which all have latent pacemaker activity.
Option B incorrectly includes ventricular myocardium, which lacks automaticity.
Option C incorrectly includes atrial myocardium, which also lacks intrinsic automaticity.
Slide 10 · Transcript 10:17

questions.text: A 65-year-old man with known failure of SA node automaticity is admitted after a syncopal episode. Telemetry during the event shows a regular rhythm at 52 beats per minute with narrow QRS complexes and no identifiable P waves. Blood pressure during the episode was 88/60 mm Hg. Which of the following best identifies the origin of this rhythm?
options: An accelerated ectopic focus in the left atrial myocardium firing autonomously
The AV node acting as the dominant pacemaker following SA node failure
The SA node firing at a reduced rate due to heightened vagal tone
An escape rhythm originating in the Bundle of His at its intrinsic rate
questions.explanation:
Absent P waves with narrow QRS complexes at 52 bpm represents an AV nodal escape rhythm, in which the AV node assumes pacemaker control at its intrinsic rate (40–55 bpm) following SA node failure.
Under normal conditions the SA node fires at 60–100 bpm and suppresses all subsidiary pacemakers by overdrive suppression. When the SA node fails, the next fastest pacemaker — the AV node — takes over at 40–55 bpm. Because the His-Purkinje system remains intact, ventricular depolarization follows normal pathways, producing narrow QRS complexes. No P waves appear because the impulse no longer originates from the SA node or atria.
Option A is incorrect: the atrial myocardium has no intrinsic automaticity and cannot generate an independent ectopic focus — only the specialized conduction structures (SA node, AV node, His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers) have pacemaker activity.
Option C is incorrect: heightened vagal tone slows the SA node but does not eliminate P waves entirely; if the SA node were merely slow, P waves would still precede each QRS.
Option D is incorrect: the Bundle of His has an intrinsic rate of 25–40 bpm, well below the observed 52 bpm — the rate here falls squarely in the AV nodal range.
Slide 10 · Transcript 10:53

questions.text: Immediately after a dominant cardiac pacemaker stops firing, a subsidiary pacemaker begins to discharge at a rate measurably slower than its expected intrinsic rate. Which of the following sequences of events best explains this transiently suppressed rate?
options: Repeated depolarization accumulated intracellular Na+, which stimulated the Na+–K+ ATPase, hyperpolarizing the resting membrane potential and widening the gap to threshold
Loss of dominant pacemaker input reduced K+ conductance, depolarizing the subsidiary pacemaker cell and suppressing automaticity
Elevated intracellular Ca2+ closed funny current (If) channels prematurely, reducing the Phase 4 depolarization rate
Parasympathetic withdrawal lowered the membrane threshold, temporarily reducing the pacemaker firing rate
questions.explanation:
Overdrive suppression results from Na+ accumulation during rapid repetitive depolarization stimulating the electrogenic Na+–K+ ATPase, which hyperpolarizes the resting membrane potential by approximately 10 mV, opposing the funny current and slowing the intrinsic rate of subsidiary pacemakers.
Each action potential driven by the dominant SA node brings Na+ into subsidiary pacemaker cells. The accumulated intracellular Na+ activates the Na+–K+ ATPase, which exports 3 Na+ for every 2 K+ imported — a net outward charge transfer that hyperpolarizes the resting membrane. This hyperpolarization increases the voltage gap between resting potential and threshold, opposing If and slowing Phase 4 depolarization. As accumulated Na+ is gradually cleared after SA node failure, the subsidiary pacemaker recovers its full intrinsic rate.
Option B is incorrect: overdrive suppression is driven by Na+ accumulation and ATPase activation, not by changes in K+ conductance from loss of pacemaker input.
Option C is incorrect: overdrive suppression depends on the Na+/K+ ATPase, not on Ca2+-mediated closure of If channels.
Option D is incorrect: parasympathetic withdrawal would increase, not decrease, pacemaker rate; and threshold changes are not the mechanism here.
Slide 11 · Transcript 14:06

questions.text: Measured conduction velocities across cardiac structures show a striking pattern: the SA node conducts at less than 0.01 m/s and the AV node at 0.02–0.05 m/s, while the Purkinje network conducts at 2.0–4.0 m/s — roughly a hundredfold difference. Which of the following best accounts for this dramatic disparity?
options: The SA and AV nodes have a more depolarized resting membrane potential than the Purkinje network, inactivating Na+ channels before they can contribute to conduction
The SA and AV nodes fire at a lower intrinsic rate than the Purkinje network, leaving more time between successive impulses
The SA and AV nodes use L-type Ca2+ current to drive Phase 0 depolarization, whereas the Purkinje network relies on fast Na+ current
The SA and AV nodes generate longer action potential plateaus than the Purkinje network, extending the total depolarization cycle
questions.explanation:
The SA and AV nodes are dramatically slower conductors because their Phase 0 upstroke depends on L-type Ca2+ current rather than fast Na+ channels; conduction velocity tracks the upstroke current, not anatomy.
Fast Na+ channels produce a steeply rising Phase 0, generating a large, rapid current that depolarizes neighboring cells quickly. L-type Ca2+ channels activate more slowly and produce a less steep upstroke, resulting in slower cell-to-cell conduction. Every other cardiac structure — atrial myocardium, Bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje network, and ventricular myocardium — relies on fast Na+ channels for Phase 0 and conducts orders of magnitude faster as a result.
Option A is incorrect: while SA node resting potential is more depolarized (~−70 mV versus ventricular ~−90 mV), the lecture attributes the SA/AV node slowness specifically to Ca2+-dependent Phase 0, not to partial Na+ channel inactivation from a shifted resting potential.
Option B is incorrect: intrinsic firing rate and conduction velocity are independent properties; the lecture explicitly states conduction velocity tracks the upstroke current, not anatomy or firing rate.
Option D is incorrect: the lecture explicitly ties conduction velocity to the Phase 0 upstroke current, not to action potential duration.
Transcript 10:32

questions.text: During exercise, sympathetic activation increases heart rate. At the level of the SA node, which of the following mechanisms most directly produces this effect?
options: Sympathetic stimulation directly activates L-type Ca2+ channels, causing Phase 0 upstrokes to occur at a lower voltage threshold
Sympathetic stimulation decreases K+ conductance, raising the resting membrane potential closer to threshold
Sympathetic stimulation opens T-type Ca2+ channels earlier in Phase 4, shortening the time to threshold
Sympathetic stimulation increases the funny current (If), steepening Phase 4 depolarization so the SA node reaches threshold sooner
questions.explanation:
Sympathetic stimulation increases the funny current (If), which steepens Phase 4 depolarization and causes the SA node to reach action potential threshold more rapidly, increasing heart rate.
If channels carry mixed Na+/K+ current (predominantly inward Na+) that drives the early component of Phase 4 depolarization. When sympathetic input activates the SA node, If is enhanced — the Phase 4 slope becomes steeper and the SA node fires more frequently per unit time.
Option A is incorrect: L-type Ca2+ channels drive the Phase 0 upstroke but are not the primary target through which the autonomic nervous system regulates heart rate.
Option B is incorrect: sympathetic stimulation does not lower K+ conductance; the mechanism acts through If, not K+ channels.
Option C is incorrect: T-type Ca2+ channels are not the identified target of sympathetic rate modulation; the lecture specifically names If and the slope of Phase 4 depolarization as the regulated variables.
Slide 12 · Transcript 15:37

questions.text: The fibrous atrioventricular ring of the cardiac skeleton electrically insulates the atrial myocardium from the ventricular myocardium. Which single structure passes through this ring and serves as the only electrical connection between the atria and ventricles?
options: The AV node
The Bundle of His
The right bundle branch
The internodal tracts
questions.explanation:
The Bundle of His (A-V bundle) is the only electrical connection between the atria and ventricles; it passes through a small opening in the cardiac skeleton and is therefore the sole conduit across the insulating fibrous ring.
The cardiac skeleton and fibrous atrioventricular ring act as an electrical barrier preventing direct current flow between atrial and ventricular myocardium. The Bundle of His emerges from the AV node and traverses the small opening in this ring before dividing into the right and left bundle branches. Without it, no electrical impulse can cross from atria to ventricles regardless of SA or AV node function.
Option A, the AV node, sits on the posterior wall of the right atrium — it is upstream from the ring but does not itself pass through it; it feeds the Bundle of His, which does.
Option C, the right bundle branch, is a division of the Bundle of His located below the ring in ventricular territory — interrupting it alone causes right bundle branch block but leaves the left bundle branch as an intact A-V pathway.
Option D, the internodal tracts, connect the SA node to the AV node within the atria and do not cross the fibrous ring.
Slide 13

questions.text: What is the primary functional purpose of the physiologic delay in electrical conduction through the AV node?
options: To allow atrial contraction to eject blood into the ventricles before ventricular systole begins
To protect the ventricles from excessively high atrial firing rates during atrial tachyarrhythmias
To allow the SA node sufficient time to repolarize before generating the next action potential
To synchronize the timing of left and right ventricular depolarization
questions.explanation:
The physiologic AV nodal delay provides time for atrial contraction to eject blood into the ventricles, ensuring ventricular filling is complete before ventricular systole begins.
By slowing propagation of electrical impulses through the AV node, the heart ensures the atria contract and push blood through the AV valves into the relaxed ventricles before the electrical impulse activates ventricular myocardium. Only after this filling period does the signal reach the His-Purkinje system and trigger ventricular systole. This sequential timing maximizes stroke volume.
Option B describes a mechanism the lecture does not identify as the purpose of the AV nodal delay; the lecture specifically states the delay exists to allow atrial contraction to eject blood into the ventricles prior to ventricular systole.
Option C is incorrect: the SA node repolarizes independently based on its own ionic currents; the AV delay does not govern SA node recovery.
Option D is incorrect: simultaneous left and right ventricular activation is accomplished by the Purkinje network, not by the AV nodal delay.
Slide 15 · Transcript 16:48

questions.text: A 45-year-old woman has a sustained narrow-complex tachycardia at 165 beats per minute that does not terminate with a vagal maneuver. A drug is administered that specifically slows conduction through the AV node by blocking L-type Ca2+ channels in AV nodal cells. Which drug class does this medication belong to?
options: Class IC antiarrhythmic agents
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
Class IA antiarrhythmic agents
questions.explanation:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow AV nodal conduction by blocking L-type Ca2+ channels in AV nodal cells and are specifically used to treat supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.
AV nodal cells depend on L-type Ca2+ channels for their Phase 0 upstroke, making their conduction velocity sensitive to Ca2+ channel blockade. Non-dihydropyridine agents target these L-type channels at the AV node, slowing conduction and terminating or controlling supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.
Option A, Class IC agents, block fast Na+ channels and widen the QRS complex — they are not selective for the AV node and are not the treatment described here.
Option B, dihydropyridine CCBs, preferentially target vascular smooth muscle Ca2+ channels and have minimal effect on AV nodal conduction; they are not used for supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.
Option D, Class IA agents, block Na+ channels and prolong repolarization but do not act primarily at the AV node through L-type Ca2+ channel blockade.
Slide 23

questions.text: After an electrical impulse reaches the ventricular myocardium through the Purkinje fiber network, in which direction does depolarization spread through the ventricular wall?
options: From the base of the heart toward the apex along the interventricular septum
From epicardium to endocardium, following the distribution of coronary vessels
Simultaneously throughout the entire ventricular wall with no directional gradient
From endocardium to epicardium, beginning at the Purkinje fiber network
questions.explanation:
Ventricular depolarization begins in the endocardium — where the Purkinje fiber network ends and fuses directly with ventricular myocytes — and spreads outward toward the epicardium.
Purkinje fibers form a network within the inner third of the myocardial wall (the endocardial layer) and make direct connections with ventricular myocytes at their distal ends. They simultaneously depolarize the endocardium of both the left and right ventricles, after which the depolarization wave travels outward through the wall from endocardium to epicardium.
Option A describes a base-to-apex or septal pattern, which does not reflect the wall-direction of Purkinje-mediated depolarization.
Option B reverses the direction — repolarization travels from epicardium to endocardium, but depolarization moves outward from endocardium to epicardium.
Option C is incorrect: while both ventricles activate nearly simultaneously, within each ventricular wall the spread is directional (endocardium to epicardium), not uniform in all directions at once.
Slide 14 · Transcript 18:30

questions.text: A surface EKG lead places the positive (recording) electrode as the cathode. A wave of depolarization travels directly toward this electrode. Which of the following correctly predicts the EKG deflection?
options: A downward deflection, because the depolarization front carries negative charge toward the electrode
An upward deflection, because a depolarizing wave traveling toward the positive electrode produces a positive deflection
No deflection, because EKG electrodes measure only total transmembrane voltage, not wave direction
A biphasic deflection, because the approaching wave first generates positivity then negativity as it passes the electrode
questions.explanation:
A depolarizing wave moving toward the positive (cathode) electrode produces an upward (positive) deflection on the EKG; a repolarizing wave moving toward the cathode produces a downward deflection.
Surface EKG electrodes record extracellular potential differences. When a depolarization wave advances toward the cathode, the leading edge creates a net positive charge moving toward the electrode, yielding an upward deflection. Conversely, a repolarizing wave moving toward the cathode produces a downward deflection. Waves traveling directly toward or away from the electrode produce maximal deflections; waves perpendicular to the electrode axis produce no deflection.
Option A is incorrect: the EKG convention is that a depolarizing wave moving toward the cathode produces a positive (upward) deflection, not a downward one.
Option C is incorrect: wave direction is precisely what the EKG captures through extracellular potential differences; direction matters fundamentally.
Option D is incorrect: a single depolarization wavefront passing toward the cathode produces a single upward deflection; a biphasic pattern would require the wave to both approach and then recede in a specific geometry.
Slide 17 · Transcript 20:52

questions.text: A student reviewing a 12-lead EKG notices there is no distinct deflection corresponding to AV nodal electrical activity, even though the AV node clearly delays the impulse. Which of the following best explains this observation?
options: The AV node has too little tissue mass to generate a measurable surface voltage deflection; its conduction delay is reflected in EKG interval durations instead
The AV node fires perpendicular to all standard leads, so its vector produces no net deflection on any lead
The AV node action potential occurs simultaneously with the P wave, causing the two signals to cancel
The AV node is electrically insulated by the cardiac skeleton and generates no extracellular current
questions.explanation:
The AV node — along with the SA node, Bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje network — has too little tissue mass to generate a measurable surface deflection; its electrical activity is reflected instead in the durations of EKG intervals such as the PR interval and QRS complex.
Standard EKG deflections (P wave, QRS, T wave) reflect the depolarization and repolarization of large muscle masses — the atria and ventricles. The conduction structures have relatively little tissue mass, so their electrical activity generates insufficient extracellular current to produce visible deflections. They are not invisible on the EKG, however: the delays they produce shape the PR interval, QRS duration, and other interval measurements.
Option B is incorrect: the mass, not the vector orientation, is the reason; no combination of lead orientations would reveal AV nodal deflections because there simply is not enough tissue.
Option C is incorrect: the AV node fires after the P wave (it receives the impulse that the P wave represents); there is no simultaneous cancellation.
Option D is incorrect: the AV node is not insulated by the cardiac skeleton — it is the upstream relay to the Bundle of His, which does pass through that skeleton.
Slide 24

questions.text: A patient's EKG shows a QRS complex lasting 148 ms (normal < 120 ms). Which of the following conditions is a recognized cause of QRS widening?
options: First-degree AV block
Sinus bradycardia from increased vagal tone
Class IC antiarrhythmic drug use
ST elevation from acute myocardial ischemia
questions.explanation:
Class IC antiarrhythmic drugs widen the QRS complex by blocking fast Na+ channels in ventricular conduction tissue, slowing ventricular depolarization.
The QRS complex reflects ventricular depolarization. Any condition that delays or disrupts the spread of depolarization through the ventricles broadens the QRS. The lecture identifies four recognized causes: bundle branch block, Class IC antiarrhythmic drugs, hyperkalemia, and ectopic ventricular excitation that bypasses the normal conduction pathways.
Option A is incorrect: first-degree AV block prolongs the PR interval (reflecting slowed AV nodal conduction) but does not affect ventricular depolarization or QRS duration.
Option B is incorrect: sinus bradycardia is a rate disturbance — the QRS complex itself remains narrow because ventricular depolarization follows normal pathways.
Option D is incorrect: ST elevation reflects abnormal repolarization during the plateau phase of the ventricular action potential and does not widen the QRS complex itself.
Slide 27 · Transcript 30:15

questions.text: Although ventricular repolarization travels from epicardium to endocardium — moving away from the positive electrode in Lead II — the T wave is upright rather than downward. Which of the following correctly accounts for this?
options: Repolarization and depolarization travel in the same direction, both moving toward the recording electrode in Lead II
Epicardial cells have longer action potentials than endocardial cells, so repolarization begins in the endocardium and the wave moves toward the Lead II electrode
The T wave is produced by an inward Ca2+ current during Phase 2 that generates a separate depolarization front in epicardial cells

Two sign reversals cancel: the repolarizing wave (opposite polarity to a depolarizing wave) moves away from the cathode (opposite direction to depolarization), and the two inversions together yield a net upward deflection
questions.explanation:
The T wave is upright because two sign reversals cancel: repolarization produces the opposite polarity compared to depolarization, and the repolarizing wave moves away from the cathode rather than toward it — the two inversions together yield a net positive (upward) deflection.
Although epicardial cells depolarize last, their action potentials are shorter (~250 ms) than those of endocardial cells (~350 ms), so they repolarize first. Ventricular repolarization therefore travels from epicardium to endocardium — the reverse of depolarization. Two sign changes are at work: first, a repolarizing wave generates the opposite deflection polarity compared to a depolarizing wave; second, this repolarizing wave moves away from the Lead II cathode (opposite direction to depolarization). Each factor alone would invert the deflection, but two inversions cancel, yielding a net upward (positive) T wave.
Option A is incorrect: depolarization and repolarization travel in opposite directions through the ventricular wall — this opposition is what sets up the two-sign-reversal cancellation.
Option B describes the opposite of the actual relationship: epicardial cells have shorter action potentials (not longer), which is precisely why they repolarize first and send the repolarization wave from epicardium inward.
Option C is incorrect: the T wave reflects ventricular repolarization, not a separate depolarization current; inward Ca2+ current during Phase 2 produces the plateau, not the T wave.
Transcript 33:34

questions.text:
The figure shows four sequential phases of ventricular depolarization as recorded in Lead II. The red arrow in panel 1 represents the direction of septal depolarization. The Lead II axis is marked with its negative (⊖) and positive (⊕) poles.

Which of the following best explains why septal depolarization produces only a small downward deflection on the Lead II recording?
options: The septal vector is nearly perpendicular to the Lead II axis, generating only a minimal deflection that tilts slightly toward the negative pole
The septal vector is directed maximally away from the positive electrode, generating a large negative deflection that is then partially cancelled by atrial repolarization
Septal depolarization is initiated by the right bundle branch moving toward the positive electrode, producing an upward force that partially offsets a simultaneous downward force
Septal depolarization occurs too rapidly for the surface electrode to record a full deflection amplitude, limiting the wave height
questions.explanation:
Septal depolarization generates a vector that is nearly perpendicular to the Lead II axis; perpendicular vectors produce minimal EKG deflection, and because this vector tips slightly toward the negative pole, the result is a small downward Q wave.
Waves moving directly toward or away from the positive electrode produce maximal deflections; waves traveling perpendicular to the electrode axis produce no deflection. The septal vector in panel 1 falls nearly perpendicular to Lead II but is oriented slightly toward the negative pole, yielding a very small downward deflection rather than zero. Septal depolarization is initiated by the left bundle branch beginning in the endocardium of the left ventricle and spreading toward the right ventricle.
Option B is incorrect: a vector directed maximally away from the positive electrode would produce a large downward deflection, not a small one. The Q wave is small precisely because the vector is near-perpendicular, not maximally opposite.
Option C is incorrect: septal depolarization is initiated by the left bundle branch from the left ventricular endocardium spreading toward the right ventricle — not the right bundle branch — and the resulting vector is near-perpendicular to Lead II, not directed toward the positive electrode.
Option D is incorrect: deflection amplitude is determined by vector direction and tissue mass relative to the electrode axis, not by the speed of depolarization; the small Q wave reflects perpendicular vector orientation, not conduction velocity.
Slide 18 · Transcript 23:54
